blocks.text: 8.1.2. Open/Closed Principle (OCP)

The payments service adds wallet payments. The ticket asks for a 1.5 % fee, so the developer adds a `Wallet` record and one branch to `feeCents()`, and the fee tests pass. Two weeks later finance reports wallet money booked a day before the provider pays it out, receipts that say only "payment", and a customer whose wallet refund failed with an exception. Three other methods had their own copy of the same type check, and nothing told anyone they existed.
A module is open for extension and closed for modification when a new case is added as new code and the code that already works isn't edited. All output below is from Java 21.
A Type Check Copied Into Several Methods Still Compiles When One Copy Is Missed
The service decides each payment's fee, settlement delay, receipt text and refund route in four methods, each with its own `instanceof` chain:
Before reading the output: which of the four methods are wrong for a wallet, and which of them says so?

Card[last4=4242]             fee 320, settles in 1 day(s), receipt: card ending 4242
BankTransfer[iban=DE89-0000] fee  25, settles in 3 day(s), receipt: transfer from DE89-0000
Wallet[provider=PayCo]       fee 150, settles in 1 day(s), receipt: payment
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: cannot refund Wallet[provider=PayCo]
	at Chains.refund(Chains.java:30)
	at Chains.main(Chains.java:38)

Three are wrong, and all compile. Each chain ends in a fallback or a `throw`, and both hide the missed case. A fallback answer (`return 1`, `return "payment"`) is wrong without a sound: the wallet provider pays out after two days, so for a day the books show money that isn't there. A `throw` waits until the path runs, which for refunds is weeks later, in front of a customer.

The knowledge "what a wallet is" is spread over every method that asks. The only list of those methods is a text search for `instanceof`, which also finds every unrelated type check, and `settlementDays()` never mentions `Card` at all.
Put the Behaviour on the Type, and a New Type Is One New Class That javac Checks
Each type answers the four questions itself:
`BankTransfer` has the same shape, and the code that uses them asks only the interface:
We compile `PaymentMethod`, `Card`, `BankTransfer` and `Checkout` first. Then we compile a `Wallet` that forgets the settlement delay, against the compiled classes only:

Wallet.java:1: error: Wallet is not abstract and does not override abstract method settlementDays() in PaymentMethod
public record Wallet(String provider) implements PaymentMethod {
       ^
1 error

The missed copy is now a compile error in the new class. javac names one missing method at a time, so a class missing three needs three rounds, but it doesn't build until all are written. With `settlementDays()` returning 2 and the receipt `"wallet " + provider`, `Wallet` compiles. A small `Demo`, compiled with it, calls `Checkout.summary` and `refund` through the old `Checkout.class`:

== Checkout.class before Wallet:
c6c5cb95973471a3
fee 150, settles in 2 day(s), receipt: wallet PayCo
refund 10000 via PayCo
== Checkout.class after:
c6c5cb95973471a3

The caller's class file is byte for byte the one that was tested. The Strategy and Decorator patterns (unit 9.x) are this same move: a caller written against an interface takes implementations it has never seen.
<!-- practice 1 -->
An Interface Is Closed to a New Operation: Adding One Edits Every Implementation
Disputes now need each payment type's chargeback window. That is a new question, not a new type. Adding `int chargebackDays();` to `PaymentMethod` and recompiling our sources (error lines only):

BankTransfer.java:1: error: BankTransfer is not abstract and does not override abstract method chargebackDays() in PaymentMethod
Card.java:1: error: Card is not abstract and does not override abstract method chargebackDays() in PaymentMethod
Wallet.java:1: error: Wallet is not abstract and does not override abstract method chargebackDays() in PaymentMethod
3 errors

A partner team also ships a `GiftCard implements PaymentMethod`, compiled in its own build against the old interface. We update our three classes (a wallet has no chargebacks: 0) and run the disputes report with the partner's class file as shipped:

Card[last4=4242] chargeback window: 120 days
BankTransfer[iban=DE89-0000] chargeback window: 0 days
GiftCard[code=GC-77] -> java.lang.AbstractMethodError: Receiver class GiftCard does not define or inherit an implementation of the resolved method 'abstract int chargebackDays()' of interface PaymentMethod.
The usual way out is `default int chargebackDays() { return 120; }`. It compiles with nothing else edited, and answers for everyone:

Card[last4=4242] chargeback window: 120 days
BankTransfer[iban=DE89-0000] chargeback window: 120 days
GiftCard[code=GC-77] chargeback window: 120 days

A bank transfer has no chargebacks, so this is the silent fallback of `settlementDays()` in the first section, moved into the interface. Unit 8.1.4 covers what default methods cost an interface's design.

An interface is open only to new types. A new operation, or a new parameter on an existing one, edits every implementation, and the ones you don't own fail when the new method is called. In the chain layout of the first section, the chargeback window would have been one new method.
When the Types Are Fixed and the Operations Grow, Seal the Hierarchy and Let javac List the Switches

Card, transfer and wallet are a set the payments team owns and changes a few times a year, while finance, disputes and reporting keep adding questions about them. For that shape the first section's layout, one method per question, is right, written as switches over a sealed type (unit 2.5.3):
The wallet ticket again: `Wallet` goes into `permits`, and a case goes into `feeCents()` only.

These are the three methods that went wrong in the first section, found by the compiler instead of by finance. The chargeback window is now one new method with a switch, and no record changes. With both done:

Card[last4=4242] fee 320, 1 day(s), card ending 4242, chargeback 120 days
BankTransfer[iban=DE89-0000] fee 25, 3 day(s), transfer from DE89-0000, chargeback 0 days
Wallet[provider=PayCo] fee 150, 2 day(s), wallet PayCo, chargeback 0 days
A `default` branch would have switched the check off for that switch; unit 1.5.4 shows that, and what a caller compiled against the old `permits` list gets at run time.

So the hierarchy is closed to new types and open to new operations, where the interface is the reverse. Choose by who adds what. Types added by other teams or plug-ins need the interface: they can't edit your switches. A set of types you own, with questions that keep coming, needs the sealed type.
<!-- practice 2 -->
A Closed Pipeline Still Runs Every Extension on Its Own Threads

The module's `ConcurrentPipeline` is closed code with an extension point: it takes any `TaskProcessor<T, R>`, whose one method is `R process(T input)`, runs each item on a virtual thread, and guards its result list with a lock. A team plugs in a processor that counts the orders it sees:
Each runs through `new ConcurrentPipeline<>(processor).processAll(orders)` with 100,000 orders, three times:

orders 100000: plain field saw 89322, LongAdder saw 100000
orders 100000: plain field saw 93320, LongAdder saw 100000
orders 100000: plain field saw 88538, LongAdder saw 100000

The pipeline calls `process()` outside its lock, from many threads at once, so `seen++` loses updates (unit 6.2.1). The pipeline itself is correct, but nothing in `R process(T input)` tells an implementation that it is called concurrently. Closed code still shares its threads with every extension, so the extension point's contract has to state them.
<!-- practice 3 -->
Summary

items: **A type check copied into several methods compiles when one copy is missed.** A fallback answer is silently wrong; a `throw` fails when the path first runs.
**Behaviour on the type makes a new type one new class.** javac refuses it until every operation is written, and the callers' class files don't change.
**An interface is closed to a new operation.** Every implementation is edited; one you don't own fails with `AbstractMethodError`, and a `default` method brings back the silent fallback.
**A sealed type with exhaustive switches is the mirror image.** A new type is a compile error at every switch, and a new operation is one method. Pick the axis by who adds what.
**An extension runs on the framework's threads.** The extension point's contract says whether calls are concurrent, and the implementation holds its state accordingly.

blocks.text: Reference
What each layout makes javac do, from the runs above:

headers: Sealed type, switch in each method
rows: edit every chain; javac silent; a missed copy falls back or throws
one new class; javac refuses it while a method is missing
`permits` and every switch; javac lists each switch without `default`
edit every implementation; javac lists them; an implementation compiled against the old interface throws `AbstractMethodError` when the method is called
one new method; javac checks it covers every type
accepted; they fall back or throw

blocks.text: Challenges

items: Your `PaymentMethod` interface is implemented by four partner jars. Disputes need `chargebackDays()`. Compare a `default` method, a separate `Disputable` interface checked with `instanceof`, and a lookup table in the disputes module. Which one fails loudest when a partner adds a new type?
A rules engine has 40 rule types and 3 operations; another codebase has 3 message types and 40 operations. Pick a layout for each and count the files a typical change touches.
Rewrite `CountingProcessor` so that it is correct without `LongAdder`. What does each choice cost the pipeline's throughput?
Find a type switch in code you work on. What would have told you about the next case?

blocks.text: Design Note: Closed to What

Every design in this unit is closed to one axis of change and open to the other. The chain is cheap to add operations to and unsafe to add types to; the interface reverses that; the sealed type keeps the chain's layout and adds the compiler's check. Making code "open for extension" before a second case exists picks an axis without evidence. If the first change comes on the other axis, as the chargeback window did, it edits every implementation of the abstraction instead of adding one method.
